title: The project canvas
blurb: Describe the project canvas: its purpose, its eight elements, how it tailors the business case and how it is built and refined in workshops.
question: An executive asks for a one-page, visual version of the business case that the whole team can help build. Which PRINCE2 Agile artifact is this, and what does it contain?

teach.h: The business case on one page
teach.body: The project canvas is a one-page, visual artifact that shows the business justification for a project. Its purpose is to document why the project is worth doing, based on estimated costs against the expected benefits and value, offset by the associated risks. In PRINCE2 Agile it is the suitable replacement for (a tailoring of) the business case management product.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 6.3.2.1, Table 6.1, Glossary

teach.h: The eight elements of a PRINCE2 Agile project canvas
teach.caption: Many canvas styles exist; these are the eight PRINCE2 Agile suggests (6.3.2.1).

head: Element
Typical content
rows: Long-term outcomes, aligned with business value and sustainability objectives
Why the outcome matters to the organization
The options considered and the one chosen
Project product, epics or main features
teach.caption: Scope and benefits contents from Figure 6.3; vision and users from the project canvas workshop topics (Table 13.2).

teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile asks the canvas to outline best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios, so the project objectives and their benefits can be judged under each. If a minimum viable product is used, the canvas must identify it so that an exception can be raised if the MVP is forecast to be delivered later than expected.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 5.2, Table 6.1

teach.h: Traditional business case document versus project canvas
Project canvas workshop topics and the canvas
head: Workshop topic
Feeds this element
teach.caption: Project canvas workshop, starting up a project (13.2.4.1, Table 13.2).

teach.body: Northmoor Libraries wants an e-lending app. In starting up, executive Ruth Adeyemi leads a project canvas workshop with the project manager, the chief product owner and two developers. They agree a vision, prioritize three user groups, compare three options, and list epics with MoSCoW. Benefits are written as measurable targets with tolerance, such as more active borrowers, with best, worst and expected cases. The MVP, borrowing an e-book, is named on the canvas. In initiation the canvas is refined in more detail.

teach.text: The canvas does not remove the need for business justification: all projects still need it, and the canvas is how agile records it. Do not confuse it with the project backlog (which replaces the project product description). And outputs such as a plan or a new app go under SCOPE, not BENEFITS: a benefit is a measurable improvement.

items: Project canvas: one-page visual business justification; tailors the business case.
Eight elements: vision, business value, business options, costs, users, scope, benefits, major risks.
Purpose: costs against expected benefits and value, offset by risks.
Outline best, worst and expected cases; identify the MVP if one is used.
Built in the project canvas workshop (starting up); refined in initiation.
Maintained at stage boundaries and confirmed by the board at closure.

summary: You can now describe the project canvas, its purpose and its eight elements. You can also explain how it tailors the business case and when it is built, refined and confirmed.

A.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, which artifact is the suitable replacement for the business case?
A.why: The project canvas can serve as a suitable business case replacement in PRINCE2 Agile (6.3.1, Table 6.1).

whyNot.0: The project backlog replaces the project product description.
whyNot.1: The release map serves as the project plan and stage plan.
whyNot.3: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report and end stage report.

A.q: Which is one of the eight elements of a PRINCE2 Agile project canvas?
A.why: The canvas contains project vision, business value, business options, costs, users, scope, benefits and major risks (6.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: Velocity is a progress measure shown on burn charts and dashboards.
whyNot.1: The Definition of Done belongs to the quality practice.
whyNot.2: Delegation levels are recorded in a delegation matrix (organization practice).

A.q: What is the purpose of the project canvas?
options: To document the business justification for the project
To plan which user stories go into each team iteration
To record the status of each identified risk
To show the skills of each team member
A.why: It documents the business justification, based on estimated costs against expected benefits and value, offset by risks (Table 6.1).

whyNot.1: Iteration content is planned in team plans and the team planning workshop.
whyNot.2: Risk status is held in the risk register.
whyNot.3: Skills are mapped in the team skill matrix.

B.q: Which scenarios should the project canvas outline, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Must have, Should have and Could have cases
B.why: Table 5.2: the business case is tailored to the project canvas, which should outline best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios.

whyNot.0: Iteration, release and stage are the three timebox levels, not canvas scenarios.
whyNot.2: MoSCoW priorities apply to scope, not to business case scenarios.
whyNot.3: The canvas outlines best, worst and expected cases; a stretch case is not one of them.

B.q: A pilot project will produce an agile transformation plan. Where on the project canvas should the plan be recorded?
options: Under benefits, as a measurable improvement
Under scope, as part of the project product
Under major risks, as a threat to adoption
Under users, as a key user group
B.why: The plan is an output (a deliverable), part of the project product, so it belongs under scope; a benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome (Glossary, Figure 6.3).

whyNot.0: An output is not a benefit; a benefit is a measurable improvement perceived as an advantage.
whyNot.2: A plan the project produces is a deliverable, not a risk.
whyNot.3: Users are the people the project serves, not its deliverables.

B.q: In which workshop is the project canvas first created?
B.why: The project canvas workshop in starting up a project defines the project's core elements to create the canvas (13.2.4.1).

whyNot.0: The project initiation workshop has a 'project canvas refinement' topic: it refines an existing canvas.
whyNot.1: Release planning reviews the canvas at stage boundaries and updates the release map.
whyNot.2: The kickoff workshop focuses on team culture, skills, delegation and dashboards.

C.q:
Which two statements about the project canvas are correct?
1. It must identify the MVP, if one is used, so an exception can be raised if it is forecast late.
2. It replaces the project product description.
3. Its benefits element shows expected, measurable benefits with tolerance.
4. It is created by the delivery team in the team planning workshop.
C.why: The canvas must identify the MVP if used (Table 6.1), and its benefits element holds expected, measurable benefits with tolerance (Figure 6.3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the project backlog replaces the project product description.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: the backlog replaces the project product description, and the canvas is created in starting up.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the canvas is built in the project canvas workshop, led by the executive.

C.q: A project manager suggests dropping the business case entirely because 'agile projects just follow the backlog'. Which response reflects PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Agreed: the backlog holds the business justification
Agreed: justification moves to the release map
Disagree: tailor it to a project canvas instead
Disagree: write a full document for each iteration
C.why: All projects need business justification; PRINCE2 Agile tailors the business case to a project canvas rather than removing it (6.3.1, Table 6.1).

whyNot.0: The backlog lists requirements; it does not document costs against benefits and risks.
whyNot.1: The release map is a plan, not the business justification.
whyNot.3: A document per iteration is not required; the canvas is maintained as the project progresses.

C.q: Who leads development of the project canvas from the mandate, and in which process?
options: The project executive, in starting up a project
The chief product owner, in managing product delivery
The project manager, in closing a project
The team coach, in controlling a stage
C.why: In 'prepare the outline business case' in starting up a project, the executive leads development of the project canvas from the mandate (Table 13.1).

whyNot.1: The CPO helps define what is delivered and the project backlog; managing product delivery is team-level delivery.
whyNot.2: Closing a project is when the board confirms the updated canvas, not when it is first developed.
whyNot.3: The team coach supports delivery teams; controlling a stage is day-to-day management.

reteach.title: The business plan on a poster
reteach.question: Could you explain why your project is worth doing on a single sheet pinned to the wall?

blocks.body: Start-ups often pitch with a single poster rather than a thick plan. The project canvas does the same for a project: eight boxes that show what you want to achieve, for whom, at what cost, with what benefits and risks. Because it is short and visual, the people who will build the product can help write it and refer to it every week.

blocks.text: One page does not mean no justification. The canvas IS the agile business case: costs against benefits and value, offset by risks.

explain.body: A one-page visual business justification that tailors the business case for agile projects.

test.q: The project canvas is the agile tailoring of which management product?
test.why: The business case management product is tailored to the project canvas (Table 5.2, Table 6.1).

whyNot.0: The project brief is kept, with agile content such as flexible scope areas.
whyNot.2: The project product description is replaced by the project backlog.
whyNot.3: The benefits management approach is kept and plans frequent releases.

explain.body: Project vision, business value, business options, costs, users, scope, benefits and major risks.

test.q: Which element is part of a PRINCE2 Agile project canvas?
test.why: Users is one of the eight canvas elements (6.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: Skill levels belong in the team skill matrix.
whyNot.1: Burn-down charts show progress in an iteration.
whyNot.3: The issue register belongs to the issues practice.

explain.body: Outline best, worst and expected cases. Identify the MVP if used, so a late forecast can trigger an exception.

test.q: Why is the MVP identified on the project canvas?
options: So the board can raise an exception if it is late
So the team can skip testing for the first release
So the MVP can replace the release map
So users can approve each user story
test.why: The MVP must be identified so an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be delivered later than expected (Table 6.1).

whyNot.1: Quality checks and the Definition of Done still apply.
whyNot.2: The release map stays as the plan.
whyNot.3: Approval of individual stories is not the reason the canvas names the MVP.

explain.body: The project canvas workshop in starting up covers user groups, options, vision, benefits, risks, scope, cost and business value. The canvas is refined in initiation.

test.q: Which is a topic of the project canvas workshop?
test.why: Benefits analysis (benefits and dis-benefits, with tolerances) is a project canvas workshop topic (Table 13.2).

whyNot.0: The team skill matrix is a project kickoff workshop topic.
whyNot.1: Psychological safety is assessed in the project kickoff workshop.
whyNot.2: Iteration planning is a team planning workshop topic.
